body.head: NOVEMBER BOUGHS: WHITMAN’S INTENDED FINAL WORD

div.p: In March, 1887, Walt Whitman wrote to New York City critic Karl Knortz that, despite the “quiescent” state of his age, he was intending to publish “in collected & revised form my pieces of last four years in a little book” to be called November Boughs (uva.00550). In June, Whitman wrote to William Sloane Kennedy that the intended book would “give the pieces I have uttered the last five years” with “probably nothing new” (duk.00849). By August, an open letter published in The Pall Mall Gazette stated the miscellany would include work from the last six years along with “some new pieces” (med.00750). While the scope of work he intended to include in November Boughs changed from one letter to another, Whitman was consistent throughout 1887 in his intention to have it available for sale by the end of the year.

On his sixty-eighth birthday, May 31, 1887, Whitman mailed Lippincott’s Magazine a cluster of four poems called “November Boughs,” immediately following their rejection from London’s The Nineteenth Century (DBN 2:422; WWC 1:28). A letter to Kennedy refers to the series as “a cluster of sonnet-like bits, making one piece” (duk.00849). Lippincott’s paid Whitman fifty dollars, and the proofs were ready for publication by the first week of September: the “bits” were published in November (DBN 2:435). A manuscript available on the Walt Whitman Archive (loc.00326) shows the cobbled together proofing slips constituting the cluster—slips frequently made by Whitman’s stationer Henry Curtz for distribution among his friends and submissions to magazines. One can imagine the poet selecting poems from his wide collection of slips, playing around with their arrangement, considering their order, the ways in which they would speak to one another, and then choosing these four—“You Lingering Sparse Leaves of Me,” “Going Somewhere,” “After the Supper and Talk,” and “Not Meagre, Latent Boughs Alone”—as a special cluster for publication. Though each of these poems appears in the 1888 book, the Lippincott’s cluster prioritizes imagery of the titular boughs, opening with “lingering sparse leaves” hanging on the “winter-nearing boughs” of “some well-shorn tree,” and closing with a hopeful anticipation of “some future spring, some summer—bursting forth, / To verdant leaves” and “nourishing fruit.” In this cluster, Whitman carefully selected poems that communicated some of the recurring themes of his late-life writing and that explained his interpretation of the titular metaphor for his forthcoming miscellany, a sort of “teaser” cluster for the book whose publication was delayed for various reasons throughout 1887.

The first day of May 1888, nearly a year after sending the cluster to Lippincott’s, Traubel reminded Whitman about the newspaper and magazine attention circulating around the proposed book. “That ought to spur me on, though as you know I am not easily spurred,” Whitman replied, adding gloomily, “I’m in a pretty shaky condition, physically, right along these days—never know what may not happen overnight. I’m not afraid but I face the facts. I want the book to come out—I wouldn’t like much to delay and delay and then die off with the thing hanging fire or half done” (WWC 1:80). Soon November Boughs was taking shape. Whitman indicated “scraps” from the past three or four years, the bulk of which he had “kept carefully together” for such a purpose, would make up one quarter of the book (WWC 1:164). During this conversation, Whitman adds a sense of urgency to the publication, admitting that he was “anxious” for its release since “some day I’ll die—maybe surprise you all by a sudden disappearance: then where’ll my book be? That’s the one thing that excites me: most authors have the same dread—the dread that something or other essential that they have written may somehow become side-tracked, lost—lost forever.” Four days later, on May 20—more than a year after he first indicated an intention to print November Boughs—Whitman promised Traubel that he has “determined at last to start on the book,” but only if he could “enlist” Traubel as his “co-worker” since “I could not do these books without assistance” (WWC 1:186). Again he emphasizes urgency:
I am physically helpless; I could not do this work alone: I seem every day to be losing something—some atom of power. Now I feel as if we should commence, before the cloud that seems to threaten me falls—before I am bodily a total wreck—before I get beyond the power to follow my guides—to finish the work I have planned to do. I do not seem to lose my mental grip—I have myself that way well in hand: but the other me, the body me, has little to expect for itself in the future. Any day the slender thread may be cut—any day. Horace, we will take the book up and see it through—eh?

At this, Whitman promises Traubel that the next day he will begin laying out the text, compiled mostly from his proofing slips and offprints. Whitman also renews his proposal to involve Traubel in every aspect of the production, and he offers to pay for Traubel’s services—which Whitman calls a “sort of communism” and an “amicable arrangement”—despite the disciple’s protest about monetary compensation. Traubel wins out, appealing cryptically to “the original arrangement,” at which Whitman exclaims “By God, boy! By God!” as he holds and kisses Traubel, signifying a “solemn pact to be ratified by love.” The undertone of wedlock in the scene is striking: rather than money, Traubel will receive Whitman’s partnership in a lover’s commitment with November Boughs acting as a sort of love token between them. “Of all the people I have known or know,” Whitman concludes, “you are the most fitted to help me just now. You know books, writers, printing office customs—best of all you know me—my ways and what I need to be humored in.”

When Traubel returned the following afternoon, however, Whitman was not engrossed in producing November Boughs as promised. It was a day marked by depression as Whitman considered his dimming eyesight and weak limbs, sitting in his room “wide awake to the fact of my gathering physical disabilities” (WWC 1:187). Asked about his work on the manuscript, Whitman shook his finger at Traubel and added that, though he had the contents mostly compiled, he would still need more time to consider its arrangement. He had previously referred to a collection of “disjointed notes” that existed only in one copy in mixed manuscript and print (WWC 1:154-155). In a prescient observation—foreshadowing his literary executors’ monumental task of cataloging and publishing the vast collection of papers in his personal archive—Whitman noted that, should he die before the publication, the manuscript would lie “straggled about this room,” and again alluded to his urgent need for getting the book printed “before I light out.”

div.head: “Sands at Seventy” in November Boughs
div.p: A significant factor contributing to the delay in compiling November Boughs was Whitman’s focus on periodical publication in early 1888. Despite continued health challenges, Whitman received a fresh channel for creative work in January, when Julius Chambers and James Gordon Bennett, managing editor and owner of the New York Herald (respectively), invited the poet to contribute his poems in a regular feature that Whitman referred to as a “poetry personal column” that ran at irregular intervals from January to May 1888 (loc.07633). In total, he produced thirty-two short poems for the Herald, a contribution for which the editors paid monthly. Whitman’s daybook notes that he also sent “While Not the Past Forgetting” to the Herald, though it did not appear in print until November Boughs (DBN 2:453). A letter from Bennett says explicitly: “We have published every poem received from you and were not aware that any had been omitted,” so it is possible this poem was lost in transit or Whitman was mistaken about having sent it (loc.07524). The May 27 publication of the last poem in the Herald series coincides with the beginning of Whitman’s earnest endeavor with Traubel to prepare November Boughs for printing, with the bulk of the book’s fifty-seven poems coming from the Herald. With this greatly expanded collection of poems not focusing as intensely on the arboreal imagery of the Lippincott’s cluster, Whitman sought a new name, arriving at “Sands at Seventy” when compiling November Boughs.

“I want to take a vote on an alternative of titles for the poem section of November Boughs,” Whitman proposed over dinner on June 3, 1888 with a group of admirers that included Horace Traubel, Traubel’s fiancée Annie Montgomerie, the Harneds, and John Clifford (WWC 1:254-255). Though he had long suggested “Sands at Seventy” as the cluster’s title, he intimates that “Sands on the Shores of Seventy” might be more fitting. All those at the dinner agreed that “Sands at Seventy” was the better title, and after some friendly bantering, the poet admitted, “I was a good deal uncertain about the title until your unanimous vote removed my uncertainty.” But Whitman seems to have maintained some uncertainty about the cluster, even as the galley proofs for November Boughs were coming in, as when he greeted Traubel with a barrage of questions about the poems’ relation to his larger project:
I have been thinking a good deal about Sands at Seventy today—a good deal. I want to know whether you feel that they will be out of place in Leaves of Grass—not integral—too distinctly different in character to connect with the story? [Dr. Richard Maurice] Bucke seems pleased and satisfied—thoroughly so: do you? Has Tom said anything to you about it? How do these poems stand in relation to the whole? Have they peculiarities decided enough to isolate them?—do they in any way, the slightest way, contradict the general tenor of the book?—what I have tried to say in the Leaves so far—what has been aimed at? I am curious to know what you feel about all that—to have you tell me. (WWC 1:423-424)
Traubel met Whitman’s concern with a reassurance that the poems were marked by a unique “dignity” consonant with Leaves of Grass. This characteristic pleased the poet, who was reminded of the recently deceased Anne Gilchrist—“one of my noblest, best, friends” and “one of my wisest, cutest, profoundest, most candid critics.” Gilchrist, he recalls, also saw dignity in his poetry, and insisted, contrary to Whitman’s ample naysayers, that Leaves of Grass had “strength, power, passion, intensity, absorption, sincerity” and was “a book of health, the open air.” In Traubel’s simple confirmation that “Sands at Seventy” was a dignified collection of poems, Whitman heard posthumous approval from Gilchrist—a kind of reanimation of his dear, dead supporter that allowed her opinions to be brought to bear on his current project.

Whitman seems to have needed this support after criticism he received from longtime friend and defender William Douglas O’Connor in June and July 1888, after he sent the galley proofs of the cluster on June 23 (nyp.00608). “O’Connor kicks against them,” Whitman told Traubel, “[He] seems to regard the new poems as in some sense a contradiction of the old—alien to the earlier poems—as if I had gone back on myself in my old age” (WWC 2:9-10). Whitman objected to O’Connor’s claim that the poems focused too much on senility and feebleness, far afield from the healthy and vigorous self celebrated in Leaves of Grass—an appraisal of Whitman’s late-life writing that persists among many readers today. Instead, Whitman argued that “the pain, the sickness, the sorrow, the misery, are not too prominently paraded—not in fact predominant” and suggested that O’Connor was at fault, that his ardent supporter and originator of the “good gray poet” sobriquet “had not quite got hold of my philosophy—missed one of its important minor streams.” One could not blame O’Connor for missing a “minor stream” in “Sands at Seventy,” since the poems seem far from a cohesive unit. Recurring themes and images are less noticeable than the concision of the short “poemets”; their common attribute is their brevity, ranging from two to twenty-three lines—far briefer than, say, “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d,” “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry,” and “Song of Myself.” Their succinctness allows the poems to be contained on the page, with “Sands at Seventy” averaging three to five poems per page in the 1888 November Boughs, and only two poems—“By that Long Scan of Waves” and “Death of General Grant”—broken between pages.

But despite this formal difference between the poems in this cluster and those lengthier poems on which much of Whitman’s artistic reputation rested, the cluster directly reintroduces readers to the same Whitmanic voice, albeit older and more succinct. The first three poems identify New York settings through their “choice aboriginal names”—“Mannahatta,” “Paumanok,” and “Montauk Point”—names familiar to those who followed Whitman’s poetic project from 1855. Significantly, the cluster does not order the poems according to publication date in the Herald, hinting at Whitman’s creative intentions in ordering the poems with this prioritization of New York. Whitman still calls Manhattan “my city” and portrays himself standing on Montauk Point “seeking the shores forever” like the waves of the Atlantic. Later poems in the cluster reinforce this New York connection, including “The Wallabout Martyrs,” “Broadway,” and “Fancies at Navesink”—a cluster of eight poems within the cluster. By introducing “Sands at Seventy” with poems about recognizable New York settings, Whitman directs readers to note the frequent return to Brooklyn and Manhattan throughout, often portrayed in the poet’s memories of childhood. It is as if Whitman is declaring that, though he has lived away from New York for over twenty years—in Washington, DC, and then in Camden, New Jersey—he is still a New York poet, centering his late-life poems in the land of his birth and young manhood.

Along with the shared setting, there are certain motifs and themes running throughout “Sands at Seventy” that unify the cluster’s seemingly disparate poems. One such motif is transformation: existence’s continuation in changed form illustrated through seasons, hours of the day, evolving technologies, and political revolutions. Whitman’s poetry itself becomes a symbol of such change, since the poetry represents the man. In “A Carol Closing Sixty-Nine”镄a birthday poem that appeared in the Herald on May 21, 1888—Whitman sees his verses thematically “in joy and hope continuing on the same” from 1855. These later poems hold the same preoccupation with Nature, America, and the “me myself,” though the body is now “wreck’d, old, poor and paralyzed” (20). He indicates that the potency of “burning fires” might be less apparent under the “sluggish blood” of age, but it is not extinguished. Later, Whitman declares that the purpose of old age is “to get the final lilt of songs” and “to diagnose the shifting-delicate tints of love and pride and doubt” (28). Old age accomplishes this goal of comprehending poetry’s and life’s changing hues by examining “what it brings from all its past experiences.” Toward the end of the cluster, Whitman bids farewell to his “precedent songs,” naming many of the celebrated poems in Leaves of Grass written from his “life’s hot pulsing blood” and “personal urge and form” (37). These poems, he suggests, form a “strange procession . . . from elder years, mid-age, or youth” with “each song of mine—each utterance in the past—having its long, long history.” He can bid them farewell because of their succession: though they belong to the past, they are not separate from the poet’s present. The procession reaches back to the dawning of his poetic project and, through the prescience of old age, he can comprehend what he determines to be their final meaning well enough to say farewell.

The changing poetic style in “Sands at Seventy” centralizes the poet’s changing body, now decayed and partially paralyzed. Metaphors for infirmity are plentiful. He is, like the titular image in “The Dismantled Ship,” “old, dismasted, gray and batter’d . . . disabled, done” (37). The ship’s mast, a symbol of phallic potency, is lost; similarly, Whitman elsewhere becomes the “well-shorn tree” with “pallid banner-staves” and “pennants valueless” (36). The immobile poet lies “anchor’d” in his bedroom on Mickle Street, “rusting, mouldering,” his health and strength declining. Again, he is like the canary, a “caged bird” occupying “the lonesome room, the long forenoon,” who still manages to fill the air with a “joyous warble” despite his imprisonment (20). There is also the emphasis Whitman places on the deaths of members of his own generation, with several of the cluster’s occasional poems commemorating the recently deceased—what Whitman scholar Harold Aspiz calls “undistinguished elegies” (“So Long!” 230), overlooking their significance as the poet’s coming to terms with the vanishing of his peers. These include “The Dead Tenor” for Pasquale Brignoli (1824-1884), “The Dead Emperor” for Wilhelm I (1794-1888), “The Death of General [Ulysses S.] Grant” (1822-1885), and “Going Somewhere” for Anne Gilchrist (1828-1885). “One by one withdraw the lofty actors, / From the great play on history’s stage eterne,” laments Whitman, aware that he is of similar age and likely to die in the next few years (26).

Whitman does not confine his consideration to current events but relates his impending death to two figures from his personal past in “Old Salt Kassabone” and “The Dying Veteran.” One recognizes the visual similarities between Whitman’s confinement at Mickle Street and that of Kassabone, a ninety-year-old sailor and distant relative of the Van Velsors (Whitman’s mother’s family) who spent “the last of afternoons, the evening hours, for many a year his regular custom, / In his great arm chair by the window seated” (29). When a ship that was caught in a contrary tide breaks free, Kassabone mutters his last words: “She’s free—she’s on her destination.” These last words gain symbolic import when contextualized in the cluster with poems like “Going Somewhere” and “Continuities.” Likewise, Whitman gives the last words of “The Dying Veteran” that he “heard in boyhood” and are “likely to offend you”; they are a languished plea to return to the past, “to the sights and scenes” among which the veteran won his fame (34). “Give me my old wild battle-life again!” the poem and the veteran conclude. Once again, one can see the visual similarity between the veteran—“Large, brave, cleanly, hot-blooded”—and the poet, who described himself in his prime as “ample-limbed, a good feeder, weight a hundred and eighty pounds, full-blooded, six feet high, forty inches round the breast and back” (Leaves of Grass [1860] 141). Whitman gives two examples of last words from kindred spirits in what he believes will be his final collection, his own last printed words.

If O’Connor’s concern was that this focus on senility and death overwhelms “Sands at Seventy,” then he shared a concern expressed in the cluster by Whitman himself: “As I sit writing here, sick and grown old,” the poet bemoans, “not my least burden is that dullness of the years, querilities, / ungracious glooms, aches, lethargy, constipation, whimpering, ennui, / May filter in my daily songs” (20). The poems necessarily depict these indications of advanced age in order to be true to the man himself, but while portrayals of death and decay abound in “Sands at Seventy,” they are balanced by those of the morning, springtime, and continuance. Spring breaks into the cluster with the appearance of “The First Dandelion,” with its “trustful face” from “winter’s close emerging.” Six short poems later are glimpses of “apple orchards, the trees all cover’d with blossoms” and “the aspiring lilac bushes with profuse purple or white flowers” (“Out of May’s Shows Selected”). This last image evokes Whitman’s eminent elegy for Abraham Lincoln, “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d,” but when “Sands at Seventy” refers directly to Lincoln, it is to celebrate the anniversary of his birth, not his death (“Abraham Lincoln, Born February 12, 1809”). Later in the cluster, spring becomes the “winter’s foil,” unbinding and melting the “icy ligatures” and wafting “softness, bloom, and growth” all over the earth (33). Whitman here imagines a revivification after life’s “winter,” a time to restore the paralyzed limbs and weakened lungs, when “thine eyes, ears . . . shall wake and fill” with a full restoration of sensory pleasure. “Soon,” he writes, “a thousand forms shall rise / From these dead clods and chills as from low burial graves.” This line is one of only three in “Sands at Seventy” to end with enjambment—its hope of resurrection suspended momentarily above the deadness of earth. The dead clods from which lifeforms will arise echo the Biblical pronouncement of man as springing “from the dust of the earth” (Genesis 2:7) and likewise Whitman’s assertion of the corpse as “good manure” in “Song of Myself”. “Sands at Seventy” presents this turn from life to death to life again as an inviolable decree: “to frozen clods ever the spring’s invisible law returns, / With grass and flowers, and summer fruits and corn” (“Continuities”). November Boughs, though titularly honoring the ending of the annual cycle, and full of autumnal and wintry imagery, also implies the impending turn of the new year—the beginning of winter foreshadowing the season’s end and the beginning of springtime.

div.head: Production Begins on November Boughs
div.p: With the last of the series of poems appearing in the Herald, Whitman began setting into motion the mechanics of book production in May 1888, sending Traubel to Michael Field Benerman at the Sherman & Company printing office with a letter of introduction and instructions for proofing his manuscript.Though the letter of introduction (loc.07520) and Traubel’s notes give the printer’s name only as "Mr. Bennerman," cross-referencing 1888 city directories and the letter’s address—corner of 7th and Cherry Streets in Philadelphia—confirms his identity as Michael Field Benerman (1824-1900), a printer at the (Roger) Sherman & Co. who specialized in photographic reproductions. Benerman often worked with the Philadelphia studio of Frederick Gutekunst (1831– 1917) who photographed Whitman in 1880 and 1889 and might have introduced the two men. Whitman’s daybook contains Benerman and Sherman’s names on a printed card in April 1883 (DBN 2:312). He previously employed the Sherman office for the typesetting for Specimen Days & Collect, and praised the company in a letter to O’Connor as “the best printing office in Philadelphia” (DBN 2:297; nyp.00459). Whitman explicitly directed Traubel to give the November Boughs manuscript to the printer a few pages at a time, “only as he needs it.” Writing had become such a difficult task for the aging and weakened poet that he was concerned with even the slightest threat of losing his manuscript (WWC 1:194). Whitman intended to have the book’s copy complete before handing the publication over for mass printing and distribution to David McKay—who was then preparing Gems from Walt Whitman, a bowdlerized selection edited by poet and suffragist Elizabeth Porter Gould. Whitman had already written a letter to McKay introducing Traubel five days before his introduction to Benerman, praising Traubel’s “American born German stock,” “liberal tendencies,” and familiarity with the printing process (loc.03109). In contrast, McKay, Whitman explained, was “a canny Scotchman—thick-set, bluff, bustling, businessy,” of whom Whitman’s friends were wary (WWC 1:168). Later, he called McKay “crude, almost crusty sometimes,” but Whitman respected his meticulous care in publishing and willingness to work with the author’s vision (WWC 1:206). “The author is generally in the hands of the publisher,” he told Traubel; “I try not to be.” Once Benerman produced the plates of November Boughs, Traubel was to offer McKay five hundred copies for sale through his firm, with the honor of having his name listed as publisher on the title page.

Whitman moved forward with his plan to publish and distribute through McKay, but there was a slight problem with Benerman’s handling of the typesetting at the Sherman printing office. While Whitman was confident in McKay’s openness during every step of the publication process, his experiences with Benerman were less than ideal and he suggested offering the job to another Philadelphia printing office belonging to Irish-born George Sloan Ferguson, whose company would set type for less than two dollars per page The firm was called Ferguson Brothers & Company, since Ferguson was formerly in a partnership with his brother, James McIntire “Commodore” Ferguson, who died in 1885 (see Commodore Ferguson’s obituary in the November 16, 1885, Philadelphia Inquirer). (WWC 1:206). Ferguson was willing to follow Whitman’s direction for Traubel to work as intermediary between the poet and the typesetters directly, even allowing Traubel onto the composing room’s floor, the liberty that Benerman had denied the poet’s amanuensis. The arrangement was finalized on May 28 and a contract signed the next day, though Whitman refused to pay the full fifty-dollar fee in advance: “I am willing to pay a good instalment when the work is half done and the entire sum remaining on the completion of the plates” (WWC 1:221, 1:226). The compositor agreed to the arrangement.

The next day, along with the signed contract, Traubel delivered to Ferguson the manuscripts for the prefatory essay, “A Backward Glance O’er Travel’d Roads,” and the “Sands at Seventy” poems. When proofs came back to Whitman by the end of the week, he pronounced them “the best I have ever received,” and added that the printers “must be first-class” (WWC 1:242). Ferguson went on to create the plates for Complete Poems & Prose (1888), Good-Bye My Fancy (1891), and the final editions of Leaves of Grass (see Folsom 65-66). Wanting to stay connected to the workmen setting his type, Whitman wrote their names in his daybook: [Charles S.] Myrick in the composition room, Brown in the press room, and James in the electrotype room (DBN 2:498). About these workmen and his proofreader, Whitman later declared, “I never fell into better hands than these. . . . I always have a suspicion that these printfellows anyhow crown all the rest” (WWC 1:122). Once the proof sheets were passing back and forth between poet and printing office, Whitman began including notes specifically to the proofreader and compositor—often just to convey his gratitude for their “first-class” work. This communication with the printers seemed to enliven Whitman, bringing him back to the liveliness of his early-career newspaper work and his direct energetic interaction with the typesetters for the 1860 Leaves. “He seems by instinct to catch the printer’s aberrations,” Traubel records, noting Whitman’s reliance on his “general feeling about a piece when it comes back to me in type” (WWC 2:35). Traubel also declares that Whitman “is stubborn about having his punctuation, abbreviations and general arrangement strictly followed,” reminding one of Whitman’s eccentric punctuation in the various editions of Leaves of Grass (WWC 1:358). To meet Whitman’s proposed publishing schedule, Ferguson hired two temporary workers. However, it soon became obvious that Whitman would not be able to hold to the publishing schedule of November Boughs. By the beginning of June, Ferguson laid off the additional help, much to Whitman’s embarrassment (WWC 1:242-243).

div.head: “A Backward Glance” in November Boughs
div.p:
Work progressed on November Boughs throughout the end of May and into June 1888. Whitman was especially eager to have Ferguson set his introductory essay, a composite work that biographer Justin Kaplan calls “a summary and justification of [Whitman’s] life in poetry” and “the last of his many critical declarations and farewells” (20). Traubel dutifully carried manuscripts and proofing sheets back and forth. In an act of literary surgery, Whitman stitched together three essays about the creative process informing Leaves of Grass that had appeared in various newspapers and magazines into one essay called “A Backward Glance O’er Travel’d Roads.” Readers of the London publication of Democratic Vistas, and Other Papers earlier in 1888 encountered them still as separate pieces: “My Book and I,” “A Backward Glance on My Own Road,” and “How I Made a Book.” Aside from its title, however, the essay in November Boughs uses little of the material from “A Backward Glance on My Own Road,” and instead derives mostly from “My Book and I,” which opens the essay, and “How I Made a Book,” which closes it, with edits throughout. Traubel recorded the typographers calling Whitman’s copyediting notation “peculiar but interesting, and always clear,” indicating perhaps a generational difference between the old newspaperman and his younger compositors (WWC 1:238). In turn, Whitman was pleased with the essay’s typesetting, and the responsiveness of the Ferguson office in meeting his demands, such as when he requested the essay be edited to leave some blank space at its conclusion. “I like chapters in books to end short of a page,” he told Traubel; “it pleases my eye better so” (WWC 1:37). The final form of the essay leaves exactly seven lines of blank space, as Whitman directed (fig. 1).
“[A]s I nigh my three-score-and-ten,” Whitman confesses in “A Backward Glance,” “I live largely on memory.” He refers to his poems as “complete,” and writes that he is “curious to review them in the light of their own (at the time unconscious, or mostly unconscious) intentions, with certain unfoldings of the thirty years they seek to embody.” But the poems in Leaves of Grass do not merely encapsulate the years from 1850 to 1880; they are the embodiment of the poet himself: “…the trunk and centre whence [Leaves] was to radiate, and to which all should return from straying however far a distance, must be an identical body and soul, a personality—which personality, after many considerations and ponderings I deliberately settled should be myself—indeed could not be any other.” This review of the development of his poetic theory informing Leaves of Grass is a review of the personality of the poet himself, since the book captures this conjunction of his body and soul: “in the centre of all, and object of all, stands the Human Being, towards whose heroic and spiritual evolution poems and everything directly and indirectly tend, Old World or New.” It is perhaps in an effort to show that his mission for Leaves of Grass had not changed much as the poet passed from middle to old age that “Sands at Seventy” included a poem extracted from the 1867 edition, “Small the Theme of My Chant,” that praises “One's self—a simple, separate person.” To write about the poems is to write about the poet, argues “A Backward Glance,” if one accepts the poet’s proposition that the poems are identical with his biological and spiritual selfhood—if lines are erased between literary persona and the living man.

Whitman contends that the selfhood depicted in the poems was not to be an idealized form of the poet. Instead, poetry is to express “the true use for the imaginative faculty of modern times” that lends “ultimate vivification to facts, to science, and to common lives, endowing them with the glows and glories and final illustriousness which belong to every real thing, and to real things only” (7-8). Though some readers may argue that Leaves of Grass conveys only the poet’s larger-than-life ego, “A Backward Glance” reviews the poems “in the light of their own intentions,” emphasizing their factuality and emphasis on the common, workaday life of their subject. Whatever egotism they exude, the essay suggests, is only the glorification and illustration of an average person, a pride “indispensable to an American” without being “inconsistent with obedience, humility, deference, and self-questioning” (15). Whitman’s lifelong poetic project is devoted to finding the sacred in the mundane, the hero in the ordinary subject, and building America upward from the proud democratic individual.

“A Backward Glance” stresses that Whitman’s project is not confined to the 1855 edition of Leaves of Grass: “I would sing, and leave out or put in, quite solely with reference to America and to-day” (7). Each subsequent revision of his central work was mindful of a national ongoing present, with each edition of Leaves of Grass becoming, as Folsom offers, “a shifting series of quite different texts—each one responding to a particular biographical and cultural moment—instead of a single book” (6). “A Backward Glance” proposes that “the chief trait of any given poet is always the spirit he brings to the observation of Humanity and Nature,” with particular attention given to “up to how recent a date is the song carried.” Though Whitman’s readers are often not as enthused about the late life poems collected in the “Sands at Seventy” and “Good-Bye My Fancy” annexes as they are his earlier poetry, the poetic documentation of an aging self is indispensable to Whitman’s larger project, since he ages alongside the aging nation. Whitman’s first stroke at age fifty-four coincided with the financial Panic of 1873—and both the poet and the United States were still in a state of depression three years later during the nation’s centennial celebrations. “Deciphering Whitman’s late work,” argues Whitman scholar Anton Vander Zee, “requires that we seek to understand precisely how it tracks the decay of both his body and his dream for America” (“Whitman Lately”). The late poems continue the mystical and egotistical transcribing and embodiment of self that was initiated in the first edition of Leaves of Grass and is consistently present throughout the many emendations of and additions to it, but they temper the self-assurance and arrogance with the reality of decay and uncertainty. “To-day and here personal force is behind everything, just the same,” states a somewhat defiant Whitman (15).

Whitman says he intended the first edition of Leaves of Grass to celebrate a dawning of the self, “to be in spirit the poems of the morning” that were “mainly written in the sunny forenoon and early midday of my life” (16). November Boughs, and later Good-Bye My Fancy, are then to celebrate and include the poems of the evening. This is depicted in the Table of Contents for November Boughs which includes entries like “After the Dazzle of Day,” “A Prairie Sunset,” “Twilight,” and “An Evening Lull”—all of which were part of the “Sands at Seventy” annex folded into Leaves of Grass—giving the deathbed collection a complete dawn-to-dusk trajectory. “‘Leaves of Grass’ indeed,” Whitman reiterates, “has mainly been the outcropping of my own emotional and other personal nature—an attempt, from first to last, to put a Person, a human being (myself, in the latter half of the Nineteenth Century, in America,) freely, fully and truly on record” (18, emphasis in original). The earlier editions were the first to put this human being on the page, to introduce readers to a subject occupying particular spaces and points in time. This subject then ages, experiences war, loss of love, and loss of health. He relocates, gains some notoriety, then declines toward death. “I felt it all as positively then in my young days as I do now in my old ones,” writes that subject and poet, whose poetry seeks in 1888, as it did in 1855, to “be or connive at an implicit belief in the wisdom, health, mystery, beauty of every process, every concrete object, every human or other existence” (17). Laying the stress on each “every” in that sentence, one can see the necessity of including the aging process and the aging human body in this omnivorous celebration of the self. The necessity of opening November Boughs with “A Backward Glance” also becomes apparent, since the essay introduces the following “Sands at Seventy” poems as a continuation of Whitman’s larger project, rather than an ancillary publication. As he told Traubel in response to O’Connor’s criticism, if “the new chapter of my story fits with the chapter just before it, as I am confident it does, I am satisfied” (WWC 2:9-10). He added that, regardless of the opinions of others, “in the end I must go my own road with such light as I have,” since “if I thought anything in my last work disgraced the Leaves as it stood in its prime—ran counter to the original statement of the book, from which I am conscious of no deviation whatever—I would end the whole thing here and now without a single regret.” November Boughs’ introductory essay therefore aims at correcting the O’Connors of Whitman’s readership, those who misunderstand the nature of the twilight “Sands at Seventy” and do not grasp the cluster’s relation to the more vivacious noonday poems of Leaves of Grass.

div.head: Elias Hicks in November Boughs
div.p: As well as helping to situate November Boughs within the larger project of Whitman’s work, the placement of “A Backward Glance” at the beginning of the book reinforces the reader’s experience of Whitman’s miscellany as a collection of interrelated poetry and prose. It was not the only prose component of November Boughs to be cobbled together from existing material for inclusion in the miscellany. The book’s closing essay on the controversial Long Island Quaker preacher and reformer Elias Hicks has a much more complicated, though similar, composition history. As early as April 1887, Whitman writes that he is “writing & collating a paper ab’t Elias Hicks” (loc.02024). By January 1888, Whitman considered the essay an integral part of November Boughs, writing to O’Connor that “I want to print a little 15 or 20 page Annex to L of G—Also a sketch of Elias Hicks—but don’t know when” (nyp.00688). Whitman had a large collection of notes and memorabilia related to Hicks in the sea of papers on his bedroom floor, so the essay’s composition relied chiefly on assembling and editing this archive into a coherent narrative. Since nearly all of the book’s contents had been previously published—including the essays forming “A Backward Glance”—the Hicks tribute was the only major component that needed to be composed, copied, and proofed before the book could go to press. The task was easier said than done. On June 1, Traubel asked Whitman how the tribute was going and whether it would be ready for the imminent publication of November Boughs. Whitman responded by suggesting the piece would be an appropriate contribution to the work, but that he felt “it lacks somehow that something or other in substance which will go to make it satisfactory to me at last” (WWC 1:247). Later, Whitman complained to Traubel that, while the essay would add much-needed material to the book’s page count, it still had a “fragmentary, discursive character” (WWC 1:265). At this point, Whitman did not feel bound to include the essay: “shall not feel guilty if it cannot be managed; if the book must be smaller then it must,” he told Traubel. Three days later, when the printers had finished November Boughs’ proof sheets—with the sole exception of the Hicks piece—Whitman suggested that the essay appear later as a separate “volumet” and November Boughs proceed without it (WWC 1:283). The “Sands at Seventy” poems and the selection of magazine prose brought the collection to about a hundred pages, so the absence of the tribute might have been an unfelt omission, especially since, in his literary executors’ estimation, the poems were to be the book’s major appeal for readers.

Whitman’s indifference to the essay’s inclusion, meanwhile, vacillated with an almost obsessive fixation on the piece, which had become the daily topic of conversation with Traubel and a constant allusion in his outgoing correspondence. Over the course of June and into July, Whitman developed this preoccupation with Hicks into the fulfillment of an obligation to his parents: “I am afraid if I don’t pay my debt to Hicks now I will never do it at all. And it is a sort of filial debt, too—a debt I owe my father, who loved Hicks” (WWC 1:374); “It was through my mother that I learned of Hicks: when she found I liked to hear about him she seemed to like to speak” (WWC 2:114). His grandparents also knew the Quaker preacher, and Whitman wanted to honor them and their “habitats” on Long Island (WWC 2:191). Indeed, he was devoted to this composition with a sort of prophetic determination: “I have got to look upon myself as sort of chosen to do a job as the Hicksite historian. I have seemed, to myself at least, to be particularly equipped for doing just this thing and doing it as it should be done—have felt that no one else living is exactly so well appointed for it” (WWC 2:18). As a result, Whitman increasingly left much of the proofing to Traubel and fell behind in meeting deadlines with his printers, exerting his remaining energy—in precious supply given the dramatic fluctuations of his health—on compiling the Hicks tribute. “Some evening,” he told Traubel, who seemed not to understand the poet’s fixation, “you will come here to be told that I have pitched the Hicks into the fire. If it eludes me much longer, fools me, rejects me” (WWC 2:11). Whitman rationalized this complication to the schedule for the book’s release: “Hicks is entitled to my best—not my worst. My best would be too little—my worst would be an insult.” On July twenty-second, Richard Maurice Bucke warned Whitman not to delay publication any longer on account of the Hicks tribute, suggesting that the fixation was too taxing on his already-fragile health. “Let Traubel have it,” he suggests, “and tell him to alter nothing except where necessary to make sense and connection, and let it be printed and the book brought to an end” (loc.07215). Two days later, Whitman responded to Bucke, announcing that the Hicks piece was in the printer’s hands. He tried to assure the doctor that, thanks to Traubel’s assistance, “I have not worried at it . . . indeed, it has been more benefit to me than hurt” (loc.07646). Galley proofs were delivered the following day (loc.07647), to which he added material over the next couple of weeks. The book’s galleys were completed by the last day of July, 1888 (WWC 2:64).

Whitman managed to create a twenty-one page “broken memorandum” of “disjointed fragments,” that Whitman himself titularly denigrates as “notes (such as they are)” (November Boughs 119). The tribute begins by contextualizing Hicks’s long life through a catalogue of notable events and leading names from 1750 to 1830 in culture, science, and politics, presented as “pictures that dart upon me even as I speak, and glow and mix and coruscate and fade like aurora borealis.” Against this colorful timeline, Whitman juxtaposes “a curious quiet yet busy life centered in a little country village on Long Island and within sound on still nights of the mystic surf-beat of the sea,” here honoring the “habitat” of his grandparents alluded to above, his great-grandfather Whitman “being often with Elias” in childhood. Whitman quotes extensively from the posthumous Journal of the Life and Religious Labours of Elias Hicks (New York: Isaac T. Hopper, 1832), with large block quotes occupying most of five pages. He goes so far as to implore the reader to purchase the Hopper book, despite its “dryness and mere dates, absence of emotionality or literary quality.” The selections deal chiefly with Hicks’s morality and the spiritual experiences that helped inform his radical pacifism and prioritizing of individual Inner Light. Whitman uses these passages for explicit comparison to Jesus, who, like Hicks, was a carpenter and wandering preacher who preferred speaking in the open air.

Whitman recalls attending one of Hicks’s last speaking engagements in 1829. Hicks was about eighty and Whitman is careful to note his “good bodily health and strength” that contrasted with the poet’s own condition, until shortly thereafter when “Elias was paralyzed and died,” mirroring Whitman’s own paralysis and impending demise. He recalls the eagerness of his own parents, putting their younger children to bed after a day of work, and taking ten-year-old Walt along to the meeting “as a special reward” since “I had been behaving well that day.” Despite Hicks’s fondness for outdoor preaching, this meeting was held in the “handsome ballroom” of the Morrison Hotel in Brooklyn Heights. Whitman’s conjuring up of the scene includes several assurances of his memory—“I can recall that meeting yet,” “I can almost see him and the whole scene now”—but notes that “I cannot repeat, hardly suggest the sermon,” though he supplies some quotes from memory in a footnote, including words of advice given to his father. To develop his presentation of Hicks’s theology, Whitman includes lengthy quotations from an 1828 sermon and an 1830 letter.

But theology is not Whitman’s focus; rather, the sermon and the letter both serve to illustrate Hicks’s celebrated ability in oratory, an influence on Whitman’s poetic style that scholars and readers have long noted (see Kaplan 69). When recalling the sermon he heard all those decades ago, Whitman’s inability to recall the message does not hinder his recollection of its effect. He notes Hicks’s “pleading, tender, nearly agonizing conviction, and magnetic stream of natural eloquence” (128). In Hicks’s skill in reaching his audience, “all minds and natures, all emotions high or low, gentle or simple, yield[ing] entirely without exception,” one can hear something of Whitman’s universal appeal to his readers in Leaves of Grass—“I and mine do not convince by arguments, similes, rhymes, / We convince by our presence.” Hicks’s preaching, Whitman’s tribute proposes, was not powerful because of the words, but because of the communication of soul to soul or light to light, a proclamation of “the universal church, in the soul of man, invisibly rapt, ever-waiting, ever responding to universal truths.” As scholar and editor J. R. LeMaster argues, Whitman “could not let go of the Quaker idea of the ‘inner light’ and of oratory as a medium for addressing the moral and spiritual condition of his fellow human beings” (99). What Hicks communicated, according to Whitman, was far more than the controversial doctrines at the heart of the rift among the Friends from which his reputation became inextricable; he communicated a sense, an affection, that was moral by virtue of its universal appeal and magnetic influence. In saying as much about Hicks’s influence so late in life, Whitman subtly argues for the same in his poetics—what he called Nature’s “invisible spiritual results, just as real and definite as the visible” in “A Backward Glance O’er Travel’d Roads.” This is perhaps another reason for his fixation on compiling the notes and including them in November Boughs.

Of equal importance to Whitman was the book’s inclusion of an engraving of Hicks, based on a painting by Henry Inman . Once the galleys for the text were in hand, Traubel depicts Whitman intently shifting around the contents to get the essay to begin on an odd page that would allow for an image’s placement on a facing even page (WWC 2:64). Originally, Whitman wanted to include a photograph of a bust of Hicks made by artist and friend Sidney Morse that decorated his home’s front parlor, but when the photographs of the bust taken by Frank Harned failed to meet his standards, Whitman selected the Inman engraving (“better adapted to our uses in the book”) from his assorted Hicks memorabilia (WWC 2:41). Whitman also wanted to include a photo of a Morse bust of himself as the frontispiece. Though it was not used in November Boughs, the photo was included the following year in Traubel’s edited collection, Camden’s Compliment to Walt Whitman (David McKay, 1889). Of the omission of Harned’s photographs of Morse’s busts, Whitman quipped to Traubel, "Things don’t always work out, sometimes they work in" (WWC 1:283). According to the brief “Recollection of Elias Hicks” in Specimen Days, Whitman received this copy of the image on June 8, 1880 from Elisa Seaman Leggett, who wrote, “I hear that you contemplate writing or speaking about him, and I wonder’d whether you had a picture of him.” Whitman was already acquainted with Inman’s portrait, since he refers to it in a Brooklyn Daily Times journalistic piece in June 1857 (Noverr 43). The caption in November Boughs confirms that Whitman considered it a good likeness based on his childhood memories, although Traubel records Whitman claiming to remember Hicks “as a presence rather than in outline as a concrete body,” admitting “I was too young when I saw Hicks” (WWC 2:45). Whitman then justifies using Inman’s image, since he was “a famous man in his day” and perhaps “one of the greatest of the artists”: this portrait of Hicks being “as good as it is rare—and it is rare indeed.”

In discussing his reasons for including Inman’s portrait, Whitman seems to have desired not only to honor his connections to the preacher, but to shock his readership. Surely modern readers also find his reasoning unsettling; indeed, when Justin Kaplan quotes this passage from Traubel, he generously omits the first sentence:
[The Inman portrait] makes him look like a cross between an Injun and a Nigger, without a drop of white blood in his veins. There’s one reason in particular why I want this picture to appear. With the damnable unreason of a sect the Quakers—too many of them—are fiercely opposed to pictures, music, in their houses. I want this head, therefore to flaunt itself right in the faces of the Quakers who see this book—who read November Boughs.(WWC 2:125)
We know from Traubel’s notes that at least one Quaker, Sarah Bunting Brotherton, did see the book and was particularly drawn to the Hicks essay.Though Traubel gives only her surname, Whitman’s daybook records Brotherton’s purchase of November Boughs and gives her address at 553 N. 16th street in Philadelphia. Thanks to city records from 1888, we know that this “Quaker lady” is Sarah Bunting Brotherton (1833-1892), widow of Philadelphia physician Jacob Lundy Brotherton (1810- 1887). Both are buried in Friends Cemetery in Randolph, New Jersey. When she visited Whitman on November 30, 1888, she expressed only support—gifting the poet a gold piece—and does not seem to have mentioned the engraving, either to praise or to condemn it (see WWC 3:209). Ferguson printed both the frontispiece and the Hicks engraving (DBN 2:499), and it is worth noting that, apart from Whitman’s image, Hicks’s face is the book’s only other illustration. Indeed, while Whitman’s editions often featured illustrations of the poet—going back to the famous 1855 frontispiece—Hicks is the only other person whose image Whitman ever included in a book, an honor not even awarded to the poet’s sainted mother.

Even into September Whitman was not fully satisfied with the appearance of the image, which Ferguson had repeatedly printed and adjusted. On September 8, about a month before the book’s release, Whitman told Traubel that “I can see defects; this forehead, for instance, not quite as it should be,” but conceded a favorable “general notion,” since “it’s not so damned bad as it might be” (WWC 2:280). After November Boughs was completed and up for sale, Kennedy released a review that mentioned the “rare portrait of Elias Hicks,” a reference that Traubel says was “ridiculed” by McKay (WWC 2:508). “That’s the business point of view,” Whitman responded, “I think the head a good one, don’t you?” This seems to be Whitman’s final word on the image of the Quaker preacher that demanded so much attention for months leading up to his book’s release. Producing both the image and the notes put a tremendous strain on the aging poet, and while Whitman reflected that “the Hicks piece might interest a few Quakers—at any rate,” he adds, “somebody had to do the job and I volunteered as the victim” (WWC 2:247).

Whitman sacrificed his rare awake, focused, and comfortable moments from May to October 1888 to this Hicks essay and its illustration. November Boughs’ concluding twenty-two pages demanded far more from him than the rest of the miscellany, since the earlier contents were largely unchanged from their original newspaper and magazine publications.Whitman’s agreement not to release the miscellany until the Century Illustrated Magazine published “Last of the War Cases”—notes from the Civil War that appear in November Boughs just before the Hicks essay—also delayed the book’s release until October 1888. Century purchased the piece in 1886 but kept it back for two years (see lloc.07530). In an August letter to his sister-in-law Louisa Orr Whitman, he calls the tribute “quite a long but very hurried & scratchy paper,” a condition he attributes to its compositional coincidence with his ill health (loc.07654). “Best to hurry it done right off,” he confesses. In its final form, Whitman apologizes for the “broken memorandum” on Hicks, stating that the form mirrors his own, alluding to his “war-paralysis, dulling me from putting the notes in shape and threatening my further action, head or body” (November Boughs 119). As Kaplan notes (69), “he labored against feebleness, ill health, and a wandering mind” to turn out the Hicks tribute, demonstrating the chief importance he placed on the preacher’s influence—after all, he did not write directly on Emerson, who died just five years before Whitman began organizing his annex. Whitman biographer Jerome Loving succinctly captures the connection Whitman was making in the Hicks essay (462):
He was a carpenter. Like Whitman, he had suffered and survived a stroke. And like Whitman, he had become something of a pariah for his outspoken beliefs. Furthermore, he was deeply religious without believing in churches. This quaker—like his predecessor George Fox—had stood up for these positions. After Emerson left the ministry, he wrote a lecture on George Fox. Whitman, at the other end of his literary career, wrote one on Fox too, as a postscript to the Hicks essay.
Traubel especially seems to have been moved by the essay and praised the Fox passages as showing “perfect strength and eloquence,” and even suggested to the poet, “you never went higher than that” (WWC 2:63). When Whitman responded that he always intended to speak on religion but avoided the topic, his faithful disciple rebutted, “your whole book is religion. We do not want the figures for it. We are satisfied with the spirit.” Like the great Quaker preachers he greatly admired, Whitman did not propose a form of spiritual observance, but rather a spiritual system that transcended the “figures” of denominationalism and convention. “No doubt I have said enough on the subject,” Whitman concluded, “[s]aid really all there was in me to say: a few figures more would not have helped.” The Hicks essay was, then, not only a historical reminiscence to close November Boughs, but the culmination of all he intended to say on the topic of spirituality, signaling the end of a thread that ran throughout his published writing.

Setting the Hicks piece marked Ferguson’s completion of typesetting November Boughs. Looking at the completed galleys, Whitman told Traubel of his intention to work “without pauses, stoppages, which at this stage of the game would be dangerous” (WWC 2:63). The pair immediately began discussing the binding, advertising, and distribution: “he always knows the easiest way out of printer’s puzzles,” Traubel writes. Whitman envisioned November Boughs as “a handsome plain, pocketable booklet” to retail around one dollar (loc.07655) and gave Traubel his treasured copy of Epictetus to show printer Frederick Oldach as an approximation of his vision for paperweight and binding.Epictetus. The Encheiridion. Trans. T. W. H. Rolleston. London: C. Kegan Paul and Co., 1881. With the model book came a stern warning to not leave it with the printers: “it’s a precious book to me—I don’t want to even risk losing it.” On August 31, Whitman used a sample of the paper for a note to Bucke so he could feel it for himself: “Isn’t it fine & thick? This is the untrimm’d size of page” (loc.07659). Bucke’s response on September 3 proclaims the paper to be “first class and will make a handsome book,” and encourages the poet to leave the pages untrimmed (loc.07231). A week later, Whitman writes that he and Traubel agree that untrimmed would be best, and that they have decided to bind it in wine-colored Silesia cloth, “a sort of linen—cheap” (loc.07561). Perhaps a bit hyperbolically, Bucke responds that he is “glad to hear that November Boughs will be entirely untrimmed,” since he experiences trimmed books with “a sort of horror:” “Well enough for dictionaries, text books, &c. but literature should have uncut edges” (loc.07240).This back-and-forth with Bucke illustrates how quickly Whitman moved to the physical matters of November Boughs; as soon as the Hicks piece was completed, the bookmaker in Whitman emerged once more to pore over every aspect of the book’s production.

div.head: The Prose of November Boughs
div.p:
While readers of poetry might have turned to November Boughs for the “Sands at Seventy” cluster, the twenty short essays that follow form more than two thirds of the page count. In the first, “Our Eminent Visitors, past, present, and future”—published in the November 17, 1883 issue of the Critic, and coinciding with Matthew Arnold’s visit to the United States—Whitman offers his perspective on leaders in the English literary world coming to America. He opens with a comic scene: a “worthy gentleman coming three or four thousand miles through wet and wind to speak complacently and at great length on matters of which he both entirely mistakes or knows nothing,” with an audience “equally complacent and equally at fault.” It initially strikes the reader as an odd way to open the prose collection, until one realizes that Whitman’s titular “our” is his signature capacious, American collective, and that these European “visitors,” when held as arbiters of literary taste, are presented as intruders on the development of a national style. In an argument that could have been taken directly from the 1855 preface to Leaves of Grass, Whitman proposes that “a New World literature, worthy of the name, is not to be . . . some fiction, or fancy, or bit of sentimentalism or polish’d work merely by itself, or in abstraction,” but must reflect the “symbol of America,” epitomized in a typically Whitmanian catalogue:
some colossal foundry, the flaming of the fire, the melted metal, the pounding trip-hammers, the surging crowds of workmen shifting from point to point, the murky shadows, the rolling haze, the discord, the crudeness, the deafening din, the disorder, the dross and clouds of dust, the waste and extravagance of material, the shafts of darted sunshine through the vast open roof-scuttles aloft . . .
Whitman argues that only when European artists and writers validate this workaday national image—rather than impose a foreign, aristocratic style for imitation—should their visits be welcomed and encouraged. The keynote is “reciprocity,” the “intercommunion of lands,” in which Old and New Worlds recognize their distinct traditions and artistries. When he invites the reader to consider “whether there isn’t such a thing as the distinctive genius of our democratic New World,” he suggests that such would express what sounds suspiciously like the goal of Leaves of Grass: “some invisible spine . . . resident only in the average people, in their practical life, in their physiology, in their emotions, in their nebulous yet fiery patriotism, in the armies (both sides) through the whole Secession War.” The essay’s implied premise is that Whitman’s work is the beginning of such a national project, and its position as first essay following “Sands at Seventy” emphasizes Whitman’s grand view of the importance of his life’s work.

The next essay, “The Bible as Poetry,” also from the Critic in 1883, addresses another outside influence on American culture: the Hebrew scriptures. It is again filled with implicit reference to Whitman’s poetic project. “The culminated proof of the poetry of a country,” he argues, “is the quality of its personnel, which, in any race, can never be really superior without superior poems.” This symbiosis of poetry and populace—and the emphasis on some “proof” of poetry’s cultural influence—harkens back to the 1855 preface, in which Whitman argues that “the proof of a poet is that his country absorbs him as affectionately as he has absorbed it.” The Bible as an edited collection—which “to me is the living and definite element-principle of the work, evolving everything else”—is presented as undergoing a process of collation and refinement reminiscent of the significant revisions made to Leaves of Grass. A parenthetical aside regarding martyrs ties this consideration of scripture back to Whitman’s late-life meditations: “no really great song can ever attain full purport till long after the death of its singer—till it has accrued and incorporated the many passions, many joys and sorrows, it has itself arous’d.”

The communication between Old and New Worlds threads throughout the prose in November Boughs. Whitman especially makes frequent reference to Shakespeare, who appears titularly in “What Lurks Behind Shakespeare’s Historical Plays,” “A Thought on Shakespeare,” and “George Fox and Shakespeare,” as well as in connection with the actors and orators Whitman refers to in his autobiographical reminiscences. Typical of his criticism is that Shakespeare represents “the dragon-rancors and stormy feudal splendor of mediaeval caste,” and “stands entirely for the mighty aesthetic scepters of the past, not for the spiritual and democratic, the scepters of the future.” This leaves the reader to discern where exactly one could encounter literature that is both spiritual and democratic, contemporary and future facing. Evoking what he has argued of his own writing—“a few hints, a few diffused faint clews and indirections”—Whitman claims that “the best poetic utterance . . . can merely hint, or remind, often very indirectly or at distant removes.” While Shakespeare’s works epitomize this poetic evasion for early modern England, his corpus does not communicate the reality of the New World and the current American moment. “Poetry,” after all, “is an evolution, sending out improved and ever-expanded types.” As luck would have it, Whitman implicitly reminds us, he is large and contains multitudes.

The prose in November Boughs, however, is not merely focused on cultural observations. Roughly half of the essays are personal in nature, some being entries from Whitman’s numerous personal notebooks. These include “An Indian Bureau Reminiscence,” “Some Diary Notes at Random,” “Some War Memoranda,” “The Old Bowery,” “New Orleans in 1848,” “Small Memoranda,” and “Last of the War Cases.” Of course, self-documentation is introduced in “A Backward Glance O’er Travel’d Roads,” the retrospective essay that opens November Boughs and precedes the “Sands at Seventy” poems. The essays on Hicks and Father Taylor are also heavily autobiographical, relying on Whitman’s recollections of hearing these great orators and the impressions made on his young mind. While one might assume that periodicals were mainly interested in Whitman’s poetry, he was able to sell all these reminiscences and memoranda-type material to various magazines, demonstrating that by the 1880s his literary celebrity had become such that the market was hungry for intimate details of his famed life—especially his life during the Civil War and the years leading up to the publication of Leaves of Grass. For these magazines, publishing a prose piece from Whitman—be it a critical review, a reminiscence, or even “diary notes at random”—was nearly as good as publishing his original poems.

While the prose in November Boughs might seem a jumbled assortment, the entries fit nicely within Whitman’s larger corpus, and were so considered by the poet himself, his editors, and literary executors. For example, “Some War Memoranda,” published in the January 1887 North American Review, assures readers that the contents were “jotted down at the time,” and, indeed, the entries appear to have been taken from the same journals and notebooks from which Whitman compiled Memoranda During the War in 1875. Both texts appear in Complete Poems and Prose (1888), in which Whitman bound together the 1881 edition of Leaves of Grass, November Boughs, and 1882’s Specimen Days & Collect (which, in turn, collects unpublished material, newspaper pieces, Memoranda During the War, Democratic Vistas [1871], and the prose from Two Rivulets [1876]). Later, McKay published Complete Prose Works (1892) as a companion volume to the deathbed edition of Leaves of Grass. It joins Specimen Days with the prose portions from November Boughs and Good-Bye My Fancy. Even when diary pieces appeared in newspapers prior to their inclusion in these volumes, readers familiar with Whitman’s previous work would have found them a familiar continuation of his self-documenting tendency in works like Specimen Days.

The ten-volume Complete Writings of Walt Whitman, issued posthumously by his executors, also includes Whitman’s prose. The executors released their own edition of Complete Prose Works in 1898, following a bitter contest with McKay over Whitman’s copyright. Although both the executors and McKay certainly appreciated Whitman’s prose and sought to include it in some kind of an “authorized” canon, both failed to continue a trend in Whitman’s publishing that went back to 1855: the coupling of poetry and prose in the same volume. Read aloud and as a whole, the prose “preface” to the 1855 Leaves and its poetic lines are sonically indistinguishable—one written in a very poetic prose, the other in a very prosaic poetry (according to nineteenth century standards). This juxtaposition—or rather, crucial structural interrelation—of poetry and prose reached its most experimental phase in Whitman’s Two Rivulets, containing what Whitman describes as “two flowing chains of prose and verse, emanating the real and ideal” and bound so as to match the 1876 printing of Leaves of Grass (inu.00001). Specimen Days & Collect would also later match the binding of Leaves of Grass when McKay issued the books in 1882. It is suggestive that each of the last books Whitman worked on other than the deathbed Leaves of Grass—Complete Poems & Prose, November Boughs, and Good-Bye My Fancy—join poetry and prose together, rather than separating them into two volumes determined by style—as McKay and the executors would do.

div.head: November Boughs and the Support of Friends
div.p: In his voluminous correspondence, Whitman tracks his progress through the proofing of November Boughs. For example, we know that he was nearing halfway through the galleys by June 14 (nyp.00715), was on page sixty-six on the twenty-ninth (loc.07518), and reached page ninety by mid-July (med.00852). Whitman’s paralysis and periods of bad health were only one reason for the slow pace; he was also sending galleys to O’Connor and Bucke for their input, with Bucke’s corrections taking especially long to get back to him from Canada. Because of Whitman’s preference for receiving galleys piecemeal, he was sending his friends only a few sheets at a time. Bucke had a complete set of galleys by August, at which point Whitman’s letters began asking the doctor for recommendations on binding (loc.07655). Bucke suggested that November Boughs serve as a cheaper “avant courier” of the more expensive Complete Poems & Prose that was to premiere concurrently with the smaller miscellany. Bucke argued that Whitman should focus more resources and advertising on the larger collection, which was set to include the complete text of November Boughs anyway and was far more expensive and elegant, with wide margins and illustrations throughout. “The ‘Nov. Boughs’ I think decidedly should be published at a low figure,” Bucke advises in one letter (loc.07225). Bucke, known to prefer elegant “art” bindings for editions of Whitman’s works after the poet’s death, naturally preferred the larger collection to Whitman’s “plain, pocketable booklet” that would be made redundant—in Bucke’s view—by the larger volume’s publication.

This is not to suggest that Bucke was not fond of the work contained in November Boughs. Throughout the long proofing process, Bucke frequently responded to the poet’s galleys with approbation. “I like the [November Boughs] (and especially the ‘sands’ & ‘E.H.’) more and more (the ‘Backward Glance’ and ‘Last of War Cases’ about as valuable) I think the little vol. a most admirable contribution” (duk.00536). Bucke wrote of his “great delight” in reading the proof pages containing “Slang in America,” adding that “it is one of the best, most original prose things of yours I have seen so far” (loc.07213). Traubel records Whitman’s confusion over the praise: “I do not agree with the Doctor: on the contrary I think the piece quite insignificant—not important from any point of view—nothing, the most you can make of it, to warrant Bucke’s enthusiasm” (WWC 1:461). The poet often relied on the doctor’s critical eye, so one can imagine the frustration Whitman might have felt with any opinion that seemed less helpful and more flattering. When the first bound copies of November Boughs were delivered in September, Whitman quickly sent one off to Canada with a letter gently mocking Bucke’s artistic preferences: “Well I suppose you have just rec’d the little bound Vol. Nov Boughs—& I fancy you saying ‘It looks plain & common enough—not handsome or presentable evidently at first—but let us see what it has to give us for good—if any’” (loc.07531). Once again, Bucke responded with effusive applause, calling the book “one of my most precious possessions,” and adding, “I like the way it is got up and every thing about it and consider it altogether one of the most charming books I know” (loc.07254). He seems to get in his own slight jab, alluding to the months of piecemeal proofing, saying “I shall keep it by me & look it through often (though I know about every line of it already).” Of course, Bucke was sincere in his dedication to Whitman, but the fulsome praise for November Boughs seems a quick dismissal of the little book. This is further evidenced by the executors’ collective decision in the years after Whitman’s death to forgo reissues of Whitman’s stand-alone miscellanies.

While it is true that Complete Poems & Prose was a more visually elegant volume, November Boughs is not without its embellishments. On August twenty-ninth, Charles Myrick, Ferguson’s head compositor, jokingly told Traubel that he intended to “try the old man with some new-fangled type-faces” on the title page. Looking over the proposed design, Whitman responded, “I have no objections to being tried, especially if I am tried this way and so successfully,” and he went on to praise the ingenuity and skill of his printers (WWC 2:214). Traubel previously challenged the typesetter’s use of “Celtic headlines” on the title page, referring to the intriguing spiral designs punctuating the title, a position to which Whitman concurred but the figures nonetheless remained (WWC 1:357).Whitman kept the spirals on the title page and cover of November Boughs—they also appear on the cover of Traubel’s book Camden’s Compliment to Walt Whitman (1889)—but cut them from Good-Bye My Fancy, whose title page otherwise follows the same formatting with the same typefaces as the previous miscellany. It is fitting that November Boughs, intended as the last word in a decades-long career, would feature these spiral devices reminiscent of the prehistoric carvings at Newgrange in Ireland’s County Meath. Such figures appear over millennia in cave art and cathedral labyrinths, reflecting the prevalence of
logarithmic spirals in nature—shells, tendrils, galaxies, and the forming of embryos. November Boughs is, for Whitman, the completion of the spiral: “my final word—my closing up thought” (WWC 2:300) and “the depository of many dreams and thoughts precious to me—of many sacred aspirational experiences, . . . of so many unspeakable records, reminiscences, worked into the soil of my matured life” (WWC 2:175).

Published months after his third major stroke, the miscellany reveals a self-consciously aged Whitman, spiraling toward the conclusion of his “celebration” of himself—a ritual inaugurated in print with Leaves of Grass. This is evoked here in a frontispiece of the elderly poet which mirrors the one in the first edition, but now with visible tokens of age. Indeed, the frontispieces are nearly mirror-images of one another but for the indicators of the intervening decades, forming what Folsom has called “a kind of full cycle, from the starting to the parting” (Whitman Making Books 58). “It tickles me,” Whitman told Traubel, “that that appears to be justifying itself: nobody seemed at first to like it: I stood alone: now they appear to be coming around” (WWC 3:182). The opening essay’s “Backward Glance” reacquaints readers with the spiral’s origination and charts the direction in which it has evolved, documenting the evolution of Leaves of Grass and Whitman’s theory of poetic composition. It was a journey culminating—as he thought at the time—in November Boughs, which was intended to be his final word. When November Boughs and Leaves of Grass were brought together in Complete Poems & Prose, the “Celtic headlines” were incorporated into the elaborate font of the title page, literally becoming one with Whitman’s poems and prose, preserving the spiraling consideration of Whitman’s career and discursive consideration of selfhood.

A month after sending the first bound copy to Bucke, Whitman agreed to a redesign of the binding for November Boughs. This was perhaps to retain the unique visual consideration of aging expressed in the “Celtic headlines.” Oldach had bound only one hundred copies in the style emulating Whitman’s copy of Epictetus, while the rest—nine-hundred-and-fifty copies unbound and bought from Whitman for $313.50—awaited a cover designed and paid for by McKay (DBN 2:577). The new look reproduced the font and figures from the book’s title page, and added Whitman’s signature and McKay’s printing device, stamped in gold on firm red boards. According to Whitman’s letters and Traubel’s daily notes, McKay himself proposed the new cover after agreeing to distribute the book under his imprint—and paying the poet one hundred dollars in royalties. This was an attractive proposal, since the poet had grown to find Oldach’s flexible binding “coarse & cheap” (loc.07664). It was an advantage that the publisher agreed to pay for the redesign, though Bucke had his doubts, confessing candidly, “I don’t agree with McKay as to the cover of N.B. I like it—don’t think his will be as good” (loc.07255). Even after receiving the redesigned version, which he called “McKay’s November Boughs,” Bucke admitted in a letter to Whitman that “I like your N.B. with the limp cover best” (loc.07261, emphasis in original). Traubel records McKay telling him that the old binding might appeal to “the Whitmanites,” but that “it would have no public or popular attraction.” The publisher was, after all, in a business that aimed at popular sales (WWC 2:440-441). It might not have been the redesign itself that Bucke disapproved, but the move to satisfying the popular palate—a self-conscious appeal to the commercialization of Whitman’s works—a goal so opposed to Bucke’s own artistic preferences.

As much as Whitman relied on Bucke for the ongoing editing of November Boughs, there was a closer opinion which seemed to matter more: that of Horace Traubel. Traubel himself takes credit for the idea to reproduce the title page devices on the cover, and indeed had been suggesting edits for the book ever since Whitman first had the notion of a miscellany. “I lean on you for this job,” Whitman told him in May 1888, “so you must stiffen up enough for two!” (WWC 1:205). Such statements reappear frequently in Traubel’s With Walt Whitman in Camden during his description of the gestation of November Boughs. Had they only appeared there, we might consider the possibility that the young amanuensis manipulated the facts to over-stress the old poet’s dependence on him. But such statements are also found throughout Whitman’s correspondence, especially after his stroke in early June 1888. “The new little November Boughs is slowly but steadily moving—Horace Traubel is invaluable to me in it,” he wrote to Bucke on June twenty-fourth (loc.07642). A month later, Whitman confided that he had been “unspeakably helped by Horace Traubel & by the best printers I have ever yet had.” This was a double compliment to Traubel, who functioned as liaison between the poet and the press (loc.07646). When it comes to his disciple’s involvement in the creation of November Boughs, Whitman’s correspondence supports Traubel’s notes, and adds weight to some of the tender scenes between the two men recorded during his daily visits:
I rose to go. Kissed W. for good-night. He said: “Sometime there will be a last good-night. Then you’ll have to keep up the story alone.” I said however: “But that don’t worry you: a man who isn’t afraid of life isn’t afraid of death.” He fervently answered: “No indeed! I do not worry—I am not afraid: it all belongs to the same scheme: we’ve got to see it through in the spirit of the cheerfullest faith. (WWC 2:16-17)
This touching scene, a meditation on impending death from a man who was prepared to make the transition soon, follows a more humorous conversation in which Whitman suggests that it is the goal of completing the book that keeps him alive. “If I die in the midst of things,” he laughingly told Traubel, “you may fall heir to all my work: think of that: all my work!” (WWC 2:3). With his duties as one of Whitman’s literary executors, and his tasks of preserving Whitman’s reputation postmortem, it can be fairly said that Traubel did inherit Whitman’s work of self-promotion, editing manuscripts, and compiling new collections.

Whitman desperately needed Traubel, a much younger and able man who coupled a knowledge of the publishing trade with intense devotion to the poet. “Traubel would now be his lifeline to ongoing publishing activity,” Folsom suggests, “and it turned out he was more than up to the task” (Whitman Making Books 57). Beginning the evening of June third, Whitman suffered a series of debilitating strokes that left him nearly paralyzed and his speech slurred. When Traubel visited the following afternoon, he was shocked by the poet’s good humor despite the trauma; Whitman was sitting up with Thomas Harned:
In the evening he undertook to sponge himself, in his own room, alone, and while so engaged fell to the floor, finding himself unable to move or to call for assistance, lying there, he thought, helplessly, for several hours. When asked why he did not call Mrs. Davis he said: ‘I thought best to fight it out myself.’” (WWC 1:259)
