When Harned suggested that they call for a doctor, Whitman stubbornly refused—still with a surprising amount of humor—arguing that “if the doctors come I shall not only have to fight the disease but fight them, whereas if I am left alone I have but the one foe to contend with.” Of course, geriatric falls are a serious matter, and Robert Creeley detects something of an ideological lightening of the situation by Traubel, who includes the scene “primarily for [Whitman’s] role of the Great Grey Poet rather than described as the old and vulnerable man he clearly was” (79). Despite Whitman’s protests, Harned and Traubel felt compelled to call for doctors, and sent off telegrams to Bucke and Dr. William Osler. In the evening, when Traubel returned to Mickle Street after running some errands for the poet, he found him with Harned and Bucke reading letters, discussing the latest magazine publications, and discussing the new miscellany. “This attack is a warning to us to hurry the book along all we can,” Whitman urged his executors; “I may dance my last dance any day now. So do not be afraid—we will push right on—right on—till there’s no pushing necessary, possible, any more” (WWC 1:260). As he held Traubel’s hand, Whitman blessed him and confessed his utter dependence on his faithful friend.

Into June, and despite these physical challenges, Whitman continued keeping up with his correspondence and looking over manuscripts and proofs. He even wrote a few poems, including “Now Precedent Songs, Farewell” and “An Evening Lull,” that would be included in the volume with a footnote describing how the lines were “eked out during an afternoon, June, 1888, in my seventieth year, at a critical spell of illness.” In the latter poem, Whitman expresses the relief of “three hours of peace and soothing rest” following “a week of physical anguish” and his stroke on June third. When proofreading these new poems on June 19, Whitman asked Traubel, “Do they seem to you to lack in dignity?” and added self-referentially that “they are feeble, feeble enough, like an old man who has to lean on a cane, but they belong where they are—are necessary to round my story” (WWC 1:354). The poem’s feebleness bothered Traubel, who suggested edits to Whitman’s original that read:
After a week of physical anguish, Restless and pain, and feverish heat, Towards the hapless day a calm and lull comes on, Three hours of peace and soothing rest and brain.
Something about the four-line poem offended Whitman’s disciple, and Traubel frequently recommended suggestions in his conversations with Whitman over the next few months. Traubel argued that “restless” does not mean “without rest,” and so “unrest” would be a better word choice; likewise, “hapless” means “unfortunate,” “unlucky,” or “unhappy,” and so perhaps “ending” would better convey the poet’s meaning. Traubel also suggested that the final line read “three hours of peace and soothing rest of brain” to produce a tighter symmetry. Traubel’s entry in With Walt Whitman in Camden for September 3 suggests something of the influence he was beginning to exert over the old poet, and how seriously he took his position as amanuensis and literary executor:
Had discovered other errors in N. B. I opened up the subject of an Evening Lull again, almost insisting that he change “restless” on second line to “unrest.” He said: “I never knew you to be so infernally stubborn before. Let me look at the proof again.” I handed it to him. He put on his glasses and looked at the sheet intently. Then his whole face lighted up. “Why yes, Horace—you’re right—Myrick’s right. How do you suppose I came to pass it again and again? You remember I wrote it on one of my off days.” “Now this is an on day and you correct it.” “Yes, an on day.” He laughed. Took up a pencil. “See—here goes then”—marking the correction. (WWC 2:248-249)
Bucke did not share Traubel’s insistence on the change in this poetic documentation of one of Whitman’s “off days,” since he believed that the original version gave psychological insight into Whitman’s processing of his physical decline. When Traubel mentioned this disagreement to Whitman, the poet called the doctor “a stickler for verbal inspiration,” and noted that “he raises a hell of a row if I change a comma if it once got in though it may first of all have got in in error.” While Traubel wanted the poem to be grammatically correct and free of “errors,” Bucke’s argument is not without merit: yes, “unrest” describes the poet’s inability to sleep or find comfort following the stroke, but his inability to move freely might well have made him feel “restless” (in letters, he frequently describes himself as “imprisoned” in his bedroom); yes, “the ending day” aptly describes the poem’s setting, but the poet’s physical deterioration might have elicited a pessimism in anticipating “the hapless day,” a phrase that better communicates his surprise in finding instead those precious hours of peace. Traubel seems blind to the possible correctness of Whitman’s original. As Vander Zee illustrates when discussing Traubel’s similar insistence on changes to the poem “Twilight,” “the disciple’s reverence could impede honest engagement with the late work” (“Inventing Late Whitman”).

Whitman read “An Evening Lull” to Traubel on the evening of September 9, 1888—a rare occasion, Traubel notes, since the poet “rarely reads his poems to anybody” (WWC 2:287). Although Traubel does not state explicitly why the poet chose to treat his disciple with the recitation of this poem, subsequent comments from Whitman that evening suggest that he was less than pleased with his concessions to the younger man’s frequent editing of the piece: “I don’t revise my revisions too much—polish: I don’t hold it to be principally important to develop special technical flavors. . . . I keep as far away from the mere machinery of composition as I can.” Here, Whitman seems to be agreeing with Bucke’s preference for the sincerity of unedited work. In bringing up the poem’s “errors” in his discussions with Whitman from June to October, Traubel was caught in the “mere machinery of composition,” missing the “psychological” dimension. Ultimately, however, Traubel’s edits made it into November Boughs and the final edition of Leaves of Grass.

On the same day as his first chat with Traubel regarding “An Evening Lull,” Whitman wrote to his close friend and supporter Mary Whitall Smith Costelloe: “Pretty critical a week or so ago—but Dr Bucke I consider saved my life—I want to finish my little brochure ‘November Boughs’—it is ab’t 1/3d done” (med.00835). At the end of the month, likely fearing the worst, he wrote his last will and testament, naming his three literary executors—Traubel, Bucke, and Harned—to be “absolute charged of my books, publications and copyrights, and to manage and control the same” (reproduced in WWC 1:310-312). Despite a slight recovery in late June, the strain seems to have caught up with him by July, and his letters frequently allude to his “imprisonment” in his upstairs bedroom at Mickle Street (see for example tex.00474, duk.00902, loc.03185). On the second day of July, Whitman collapsed in Traubel’s arms as the men were reviewing proof sheets. Later, Traubel deemed July 30 “one of W’s worst days,” with the poet drained completely of energy and unable to move (WWC 2:58). Still, he was able to talk about his plans for November Boughs and look over a few pages of proof.

Following the strokes in early June, Whitman began taking large doses of calomel—mercury chloride—as a sedative to aid his sleep, as he had done following his first stroke a decade earlier (prc.00032). When his caregiver Nathan Baker refused to administer more calomel without the consent of a doctor, Whitman dashed off a letter to Bucke, imploring him that “in the chronic condition I seem to be in [calomel powders] seem to bring better result than any thing else” (loc.07768). “I took calomel and calomel until it was of no effect,” he told Traubel (WWC 2:65). Unlike many nineteenth-century patients taking calomel, Whitman did not die from mercury poisoning. However, as attested by his correspondence and Traubel’s notes, the common side effects he experienced did not improve his comfort: gastric pain, cramping, vomiting, diarrhea. His letters to Bucke show that Whitman took regular large doses of calomel from 1888 until his death in 1892.See for example loc.07618, in which he asks for a dosage “a little stronger” in 1889, and loc.08015 in which he describes taking it with purgative mineral water in 1891. In November 1891, Bucke prescribed six grains of calomel, higher than the average recommended dose of .5 to 5 grains (See for example loc.07618, in which he asks for a dosage “a little stronger” in 1889, and loc.08015 in which he describes taking it with purgative mineral water in 1891. In November 1891, Bucke prescribed six grains of calomel, higher than the average recommended dose of .5 to 5 grains (loc.07126; Fenner, 525).

It would have been forgivable if Whitman abandoned plans for November Boughs at this difficult time. After all, the deadlines kept getting pushed back, the printers were growing impatient, and he could not be as involved with the publication as he had originally intended. Bucke suggested as much to Traubel, eager to see Whitman’s final edition of Leaves of Grass go into print before the poet’s death. But Traubel was shocked at the suggestion and confessed as much to Whitman: “Let them wait,” was the poet’s choked reply (WWC 1:304). Later, Whitman gave a hint as to his reason for insisting on personal involvement with the book. Naturally, the old printer was interested in the mechanics of book production, but there was something deeper about November Boughs than the excitement of the composing room. “Instead of a hinderance,” Whitman asserts, “it has been a tonic in all the dreary days”—certainly a better medicine than the calomel—adding that he would have died without the project to occupy his attention (WWC 2:36). “The siege is a long one—I don’t know how long or when or where I shall get through with it: but I am satisfied whatever eventuates so I get my book out before the curtain is rung down.” The collection of his periodical poems, their assemblage into “Sands at Seventy,” the proofing of his prose pieces, and the continuous correspondence with trusted friends regarding the galleys was a sort of art therapy for Whitman. “November Boughs was in fact Whitman’s ‘backward glance’ on a life he had always insisted was not literary but literal in its love of the people and places enshrined in his poetry,” Loving asserts (463). With its essays on Hicks, old Brooklyn, and his travels out west, the miscellany echoed Whitman’s life’s journey. It was itself life review, the therapeutic process summarized by art therapist Raquel Chapin Stephenson as one that helps the terminal patient “come to terms with both the good and bad in his or her life and allow for a final separation and acceptance of that history” (25). “Making art provides a safe, symbolic arena in which to explore,” Stephenson argues, with the resulting work functioning as “a representative of this journey and a point of admiration or discussion for curious others with whom the elder wishes to share.” In creating his public-facing life review, Whitman is always aware of these “curious others”—his readers and his close friends—who would receive his final statement of himself in November Boughs. “Whitman credited Bucke with saving his life,” Loving argues: “The other thing that probably saved him was the putting to press of November Boughs, which he couldn’t have completed without Traubel” (461). In Bucke and Traubel—those on whom the future of the publication rested—the “curious others” of readership and friends came together fully embodied. It is no wonder that the crafting of the miscellany should serve as a “tonic” for the dying poet.

It was a tonic made sweeter by the opportunity to share it with a wide group of friends. Whitman’s daybook records forty people who received November Boughs in October 1888, after McKay had finished the binding (DBN 2:474). The list includes faithfully ardent supporters like Herbert Gilchrist and William Douglas O’Connor, and fellow writers like Hamlin Garland and William Dean Howells. He was sure to honor those who had contributed in some way to the creation of the miscellany, and sent two copies to Bucke, one copy to the artist Sidney Morse (despite not using the photographs of his busts), and one to Traubel’s fiancée Annie Montgomery. For their practical support during this difficult period, Mary Davis and Drs. Wharton, Walsh, and Osler received copies as well, their names included on the list with more personal entries like Whitman’s sisters Hannah and Mary, his sister-in-law Lou, and his longtime lover Harry Stafford. Indeed, compiling the recipient list itself must have been a therapeutic life review for the old poet. Several letters from Whitman’s friends in receipt of November Boughs survive. A typical example is William Sloane Kennedy’s letter, effusively praising “the precious volume” whose arrival in the post “drew forth an exclamation of delight” (loc.02956). “The very mass is wonderful,” he added, “considering that they emanate from a semi-invalid.” Although Whitman had sent Kennedy galleys throughout the publication process, Kennedy was surprised to detect “a range & strength that I had not tho’t to be quite so marked, when I read the pieces separately as they came out.” Kennedy noted that “Sands at Seventy” was marked by “a deepening shade of the sombre” that “completes your picture of a typical man—a man complete, clear through the ‘opiate’ shades to the gates of death.” Kennedy recognized in November Boughs the closing celebration of 1855’s “Walt Whitman, an American, one of the roughs,” without which this depiction of the self would have been incomplete.

Whitman himself was pleased with November Boughs: “It is upon the whole what I wanted & planned, especially the ‘Backwards Road’ piece” he wrote to Bucke (loc.07525). Tellingly, he confided to the doctor that he thought the miscellany “not at all to itself alone, but to its place with all I have uttered & also to the future & permanency.” Rather than a detraction from his 1855 project of self-singing, every aspect of November Boughs communicated his evolving self-awareness. “The poems are striking reflections on old age,” Folsom proposes, “and everything about this book, from the color of the binding to the title to the frontispiece portrait, suggests a kind of November of the soul, the self heading into winter and death” (Whitman Making Books 57). Whitman intended it to be the final word of his lifework, after which he could hang up his hat. “I am fighting for a chance to finish the book—after that I can die in peace,” he declared (WWC 1:342). And it was a fight: the miscellany was compiled and published despite the series of strokes and subsequent loss of motor function, a further debilitating abuse of mercury chloride, his mental and physical “imprisonment” in the bedroom of the Mickle Street residence, and his necessary dependence on his nurses, housekeeper, and literary friends. But, to the surprise of most of these friends and supporters, Whitman did not die at the end of 1888, and November Boughs was not to be the final word it was intended to be. Instead, he endured—in mostly the same state of invalidism and exhaustion—for over three years, and continued his creative outpouring to newspapers and magazines, culminating in yet another compiled “final word”: 1891’s Good-Bye My Fancy.
